title: How electric vehicles could hit the accelerator
gist: Wood Mackenzie's 'electric shock' scenario models oil supply shocks, policy and battery innovation converging to lift EVs from 4% of the global vehicle fleet in 2025 to well above its 25%-by-2040 base case, cutting 2040 oil demand to 99 million b/d (5 million b/d below base case) and forcing the early closure of about 40 refineries. Neither metals nor power supply is the binding constraint — roughly US$45 billion of extra greenfield metals investment (US$25 billion of it copper) and managed charging would suffice — but both require capital to flow to high-risk jurisdictions and utilities to scale load flexibility. The scenario is anchored on China exporting deflation into emerging markets and on Japanese/Korean battery makers, not Western incumbents, funding frontier chemistries.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie's base case has battery-electric vehicles rising from 4% of the global passenger and commercial vehicle fleet in 2025 to 25% in 2040 — a fleet-share metric far below headline sales-share numbers because fleet turnover is slow.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: Anchor for oil-demand models: even aggressive EV sales leave three-quarters of the 2040 fleet burning liquid fuel in the base case.
insights.quote: We forecast EVs to jump from 4% of the global passenger and commercial vehicle fleet in 2025 to 25% in 2040.
insights.locator: Just cruising: our base case for EVs through 2040

insights.claim: The 'electric shock' scenario is built on three converging forces — oil supply shocks, policy decisions and technological innovation — rather than on any single driver, making it a useful checklist for testing whether an EV acceleration narrative is credible.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: Use the three-force test to discount single-variable EV bull cases; all three must fire for the acceleration case.
insights.quote: three forces – oil supply shocks, policy decisions and technological innovation – could converge to accelerate that growth and send EV adoption into overdrive
insights.locator: Electric vehicles (EVs) command a growing share

insights.claim: The scenario's definition of EVs excludes plug-in hybrids and counts battery-electric vehicles only, which makes its adoption numbers structurally lower than China-reported 'new energy vehicle' statistics.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: Definitional gap: cross-checking Wood Mackenzie EV shares against NEV data will systematically overstate the delta unless PHEVs are stripped out.
insights.quote: In this report, EVs refer to battery-electric vehicles only, excluding plug-in hybrids.
insights.locator: In this report, EVs refer to

insights.claim: US passenger EV sales in the first five months of 2026 fell 33% year-on-year after tax incentives were withdrawn, demonstrating that US EV demand is policy-dependent rather than self-sustaining.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: US EV volumes are a policy trade, not a secular trade — size positions in US-exposed EV supply chains to the incentive calendar.
insights.quote: In the US, passenger EV sales in the first five months of 2026 were down 33% from the same period of 2025, after tax incentives were withdrawn.
insights.locator: Just cruising: our base case for EVs through 2040

insights.claim: Europe's EV sales rose 30% in the first five months of 2026 while the US fell 33% over the identical period, the widest transatlantic divergence in the dataset and a direct consequence of opposite policy direction.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: Regional mix matters more than global EV growth for supplier earnings; Europe-weighted battery and component exposure outperformed US-weighted in 2026.
insights.quote: In Europe, EV sales were up 30% over the same period.
insights.locator: Just cruising: our base case for EVs through 2040

insights.claim: China's EV market share jumped from 33% in Q2 2025 to 42% in Q2 2026 driven by a steep downturn in gasoline car sales rather than by EV volume growth — EV volumes actually fell slightly.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: Rising EV share can mask a shrinking total auto market; share gains alone are not a revenue signal for Chinese EV makers.
insights.quote: a steep downturn in gasoline car sales lifted the market share of EVs from 33% in Q2 2025 to 42% in Q2 2026, despite a small fall in volume
insights.locator: Just cruising: our base case for EVs through 2040

insights.claim: EVs have already reached total-cost-of-ownership purchase price parity with gasoline and diesel vehicles in China, with Europe not reaching that milestone until 2030 and the US until 2033 in the base case.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: China's seven-to-ten-year TCO head start is the mechanism behind its export push — Chinese OEMs can price at parity abroad while Western OEMs cannot.
insights.quote: On a total-cost-of-ownership (TCO) basis, EVs have already reached purchase price parity with gasoline or diesel vehicles in China.
insights.locator: Just cruising: our base case for EVs through 2040

themes.theme: China as exporter of EV deflation

insights.claim: China's state-supported EV sector is structurally oversupplied, with production exceeding domestic sales by around 50% in 2025, leaving most manufacturers on thin margins and forcing them to hunt export growth.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: Structural overcapacity plus thin margins guarantees aggressive price-led export expansion — a persistent deflationary force on global EV pricing and a margin risk for Western OEMs.
insights.quote: With the explicit support of the state through government-backed loans, China’s EV sector is oversupplied. Production exceeded domestic sales by around 50% in 2025.
insights.locator: China: the global motor of faster EV adoption

insights.claim: Chinese policy measures modelled in the scenario — gasoline consumption restrictions, a full EV purchase tax exemption and larger up-front sales credits — would cut Chinese EV total cost of ownership by roughly 30% and lift China's EV sales from 8.9 million in 2025 to 29.9 million in 2040.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: A Chinese gasoline-restriction policy is the single highest-leverage watch item for global oil demand; it would remove millions of barrels of Chinese gasoline consumption.
insights.quote: These policy steps would cut the total cost of EV ownership in China by about 30%, meaning China’s EV sales would rise from 8.9 million last year to 29.9 million in 2040 under our electric shock scenario.
insights.locator: China: the global motor of faster EV adoption

insights.claim: Chinese EV manufacturing capacity rises 50% by 2035 in the scenario, with the resulting economies of scale giving Chinese manufacturers cost bases that let them undercut competitors across Global South markets.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: Emerging-market auto incumbents (Japanese and Korean brands in particular) face share loss where tariffs are absent; watch import-share data as the leading indicator.
insights.locator: China: the global motor of faster EV adoption

insights.claim: Chinese EV sales in Mexico exploded from around 3,000 units in 2023 to nearly 80,000 in 2025, taking 6% of all Mexican car sales in just two years — a live template for how fast Chinese OEMs can take an unprotected emerging market.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: Mexico is the observable proof-of-concept; a 26x volume increase in two years sets the pace to expect in other tariff-free emerging markets.
insights.quote: In Mexico, sales of Chinese EVs ballooned from around 3,000 in 2023 to nearly 80,000 in 2025. Chinese EVs now make up 6% of all Mexican car sales, a substantial feat in just two years.
insights.locator: Emerging markets: a tidal wave of Chinese EV expansion

insights.claim: Chinese EV imports cut emerging market EV costs by 28% in the scenario, letting Chinese vehicles capture nearly 30% of emerging market sales by 2040 — double their base-case share.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: Emerging-market gasoline demand, long the reliable growth engine for oil, is the volume most exposed to Chinese EV price deflation.
insights.locator: Emerging markets: a tidal wave of Chinese EV expansion

insights.claim: Chinese investment in emerging-market charging infrastructure combined with declining fossil-fuel subsidies lifts total emerging-market EV stock 85% above base case by 2040, making subsidy reform — not vehicle price alone — a decisive variable.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: Track fossil-fuel subsidy removal in large emerging economies as a direct forward indicator of EV penetration and gasoline demand destruction.
insights.locator: Emerging markets: a tidal wave of Chinese EV expansion

insights.claim: Europe's auto giants announced roughly 60,000 layoffs in 2026 alone, and that job pressure — not climate ambition — is what makes a tariff-relief-for-Chinese-investment 'grand bargain' politically plausible.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: European EV tariff policy is likely to soften in exchange for local Chinese plants; positions premised on permanent EU tariff protection are exposed.
insights.quote: So far in 2026, Europe’s auto giants have announced some 60,000 layoffs, with more potentially on the horizon.
insights.locator: Europe: a grand bargain

insights.claim: The scenario has Europe funding €10,000 EV purchase credits with a €0.12 per litre fuel tax, a budget-neutral design that simultaneously raises the running cost of internal-combustion vehicles and lowers the EV purchase price.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: A self-funding fuel-tax-to-EV-credit transfer is the mechanism to watch in fiscally constrained Europe — it double-hits refining margins and gasoline volumes.
insights.quote: Europe adopts a €0.12/litre fuel tax to fund €10,000 EV purchase credits, maintaining budget neutrality in our scenario.
insights.locator: Europe: a grand bargain

insights.claim: Combined Chinese-backed local factories, tariff reductions and fuel-tax-funded purchase credits lower European EV total cost of ownership by 23% by 2040 relative to the base case, versus a base case that already takes Europe's EV fleet share from 3% in 2025 to 35% in 2040.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: Europe already carries the highest base-case EV fleet share of the three major regions — the marginal upside there is smaller than the US in percentage terms.
insights.locator: Europe: a grand bargain

themes.theme: US: cheap oil as the anti-EV force

insights.claim: Abundant domestic oil supply is the structural reason the US has the weakest EV incentive of the major markets, with the base case taking EVs from just 3% of the US fleet today to 20% in 2040 — the lowest of the three regions modelled.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: US EV adoption is inversely levered to US oil abundance; a sustained domestic supply shock is the only fast route to US EV acceleration.
insights.quote: Abundant oil supplies mean the US has less of an incentive to shift to EVs than many other countries.
insights.locator: United States: global competition propels US EV investment skyward

insights.claim: Even a Democratic White House win in 2028 restoring EV incentives would leave tariffs on Chinese EV imports in place and direct Chinese investment in US EV manufacturing off the table, making US EV cost reduction dependent on domestic innovation rather than Chinese scale.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: Do not model a US-China EV thaw off an election outcome; the tariff wall is treated as bipartisan and structural.
insights.quote: Even if the Democrats brought back EV incentives with a White House win in 2028, tariffs on Chinese EV imports would likely remain in place. Direct Chinese investment in US EV manufacturing will probably remain off the table.
insights.locator: United States: global competition propels US EV investment skyward

insights.claim: Without advanced battery technologies the US auto sector risks ceding its home market to non-Chinese EVs — meaning the competitive threat to Detroit comes from Korean, Japanese and European entrants, not only from China.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: Tariffs against China do not protect US OEMs from the actual near-term share threat; battery-tech capability is the real moat.
insights.quote: Without advanced battery technologies, the US auto sector is at risk of ceding its home market to non-Chinese EVs and falling behind competitors internationally.
insights.locator: United States: global competition propels US EV investment skyward

insights.claim: Greenfield US EV plants using modular technologies could cut EV production costs by up to 50% from current standards, bringing US TCO parity with gasoline vehicles forward to 2031 from 2033 and leaving the 2040 US EV fleet 51% larger than base case.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: The US has the largest percentage upside of any region in the scenario — a 51% fleet delta — making it the highest-beta EV market to policy reversal.
insights.quote: Automakers launch new greenfield EV plants that employ modular technologies, reducing EV production costs by up to 50% from current standards.
insights.locator: United States: global competition propels US EV investment skyward

themes.theme: Charging infrastructure and grid load management

insights.claim: The world's 7 million public charging ports run at just 15% utilisation across all major markets as of end-2025 because the five-year charging build-out outpaced EV sales, giving near-term slack that an EV surge would rapidly consume.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: Charge-point operators are currently over-built and margin-poor; rising utilisation toward the second build-out wave is the earnings inflection to watch.
insights.quote: The five-year build-out of public charging has outpaced EV sales, leaving 15% utilisation across all major markets as of end 2025.
insights.locator: The world’s public EV charging network can absorb a surge in EVs near term

insights.claim: A second charging build-out wave under the scenario requires China to add 4 million more ports at about US$200 billion of extra investment, Europe US$108 billion for 2.7 million more ports, and the US only 500,000 additional ports — a 400-to-1 split in port counts that reflects adoption, not geography.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: Charging-hardware and installation revenue pools are overwhelmingly Chinese and European; US-listed charging pure-plays face a small addressable increment.
insights.locator: The world’s public EV charging network can absorb a surge in EVs near term

insights.claim: Managed charging, not new generation, is the binding solution to EV grid load: in Europe EV charging at peak load rises only from 0.4% of total generation capacity in 2026 to 2.6% by 2040, implying just 28 GW of additional generation capacity needed over 14 years.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: The 'EVs will break the grid' thesis is rejected on the numbers — 28 GW over 14 years is trivial versus AI data centre load; the investable constraint is software and tariff design, not turbines.
insights.quote: EV charging at times of peak load on the grid rises from 0.4% of total generation capacity in 2026 to just 2.6% by 2040. This implies a need for just 28 GW of additional generation capacity to be added over the next 14 years.
insights.locator: Load management keeps grids stable and charging prices competitive

insights.claim: Managed charging penetration is 50% in western Europe in 2025 but no more than 5% of US charging sessions, a ten-fold gap that makes the US grid far more exposed to unmanaged EV peak load.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: US utilities and demand-response vendors have the larger runway; European managed-charging programmes are already near saturation.
insights.quote: In the US, managed charging amounted to no more than 5% of charging sessions in 2025.
insights.locator: Load management keeps grids stable and charging prices competitive

insights.claim: If the US reached Europe's current 50% managed-charging participation, peak daily EV demand on the largest US grids in 2040 would be unchanged from base case even though EV electricity consumption rises 46% — load shifting fully absorbs a near-50% demand increase.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: Peak capacity and energy volume decouple entirely under managed charging — a reason to be long EV electricity volume without being long peaking capacity.
insights.quote: At 50% participation in managed charging – the current rate in Europe – peak daily EV demand on the largest US grids in 2040 would be unchanged from our base case.
insights.locator: Load management keeps grids stable and charging prices competitive

insights.claim: The scenario assumes EV owners will progressively surrender control over when their vehicles charge in exchange for cheaper home charging, making consumer acceptance of utility-controlled charging a load-bearing behavioural assumption.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: If consumers reject ceding charge control, the whole no-new-generation conclusion breaks — this is the scenario's softest assumption.
insights.quote: we expect EV owners to increasingly cede control over when their vehicles charge in return for cheaper home charging
insights.locator: Load management keeps grids stable and charging prices competitive

insights.claim: European total annual power consumption rises 44% by 2040 in the scenario, with EVs accounting for only about a third of that growth — meaning two-thirds of European load growth comes from sources other than transport electrification.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: Don't attribute European power demand growth primarily to EVs when sizing generation and grid capex opportunities.
insights.locator: Load management keeps grids stable and charging prices competitive

insights.claim: Global oil demand in 2040 is 104 million b/d in the base case — roughly current levels — but 99 million b/d under the electric shock scenario, a 5 million b/d gap that is the entire investable difference between an oil plateau and an oil decline.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: 5 million b/d is the quantified downside tail for long-dated oil; it is the number to stress-test upstream project economics against.
insights.quote: By 2040, our base case projects global oil demand at 104 million b/d, roughly its current level. In our electric shock scenario, global oil demand is 5 million b/d lower, at 99 million b/d in 2040.
insights.locator: Oil: around 40 refiners face early closure

insights.claim: Because the average refinery has 200,000 b/d capacity, a 5 million b/d transport fuel demand drop translates mechanically into the accelerated closure of around 40 refineries — refining, not upstream, absorbs the first shock.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: Refining is the highest-beta short to EV acceleration; capital-intensive assets reliant on high utilisation become loss-making before upstream feels it.
insights.quote: As the average-sized refinery has a capacity of 200,000 b/d, a 5 million b/d drop in transport fuel demand could accelerate the closure of around 40 refineries.
insights.locator: Oil: around 40 refiners face early closure

insights.claim: OECD refineries are the most at risk of early closure because of their high energy costs and carbon prices, concentrating the rationalisation in Europe and North America rather than in Asia or the Middle East.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: Geographic screen for refining shorts and for surviving-asset longs: OECD-exposed refiners carry the closure risk, low-cost non-OECD complexes take share.
insights.quote: Refineries in Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries are most at risk due to their high energy costs and carbon prices.
insights.locator: Oil: around 40 refiners face early closure

insights.claim: Global mineral reserves are more than sufficient for the electric shock scenario — the binding constraint is delivery speed, requiring about US$45 billion of additional greenfield metals investment over the next decade.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: Reframes the 'not enough metal for EVs' consensus as a capital-velocity and permitting problem, not a geology problem.
insights.quote: There are more than enough minerals globally to meet demand for EVs in our electric shock scenario. The challenge is how quickly new supply can be delivered.
insights.locator: Critical minerals: brave capital is needed to unlock supply bottlenecks

insights.claim: Copper is the single most critical bottleneck, requiring annual mine capacity additions to rise from the roughly 850 ktpa long-term average to about 960 ktpa over 2025-2040, at only about US$25 billion of additional investment against roughly US$250 billion already forecast in the base case.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: A 10% incremental capex ask on copper is small in dollars but requires a 13% step-up in annual capacity additions — the delivery risk, not the funding, is what tightens the copper market.
insights.quote: Annual mine capacity additions would have to rise from about 850 ktpa, the long-term average, to about 960 ktpa over 2025 to 2040.
insights.locator: Critical minerals: brave capital is needed to unlock supply bottlenecks

insights.claim: Incremental copper growth must come from higher-risk jurisdictions including Argentina, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Pakistan, and if Chile, Peru or the US fail to streamline permitting and keep fiscal terms competitive, that growth shifts to state-backed, risk-tolerant Chinese entities.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: Permitting reform in Chile, Peru and the US is a directly tradable geopolitical variable — failure hands marginal copper supply control to Chinese state capital.
insights.quote: If established mining regions such as Chile, Peru or the US fail to streamline permitting and maintain competitive fiscal terms, a larger share of future growth will shift towards state-backed, risk-tolerant Chinese entities.
insights.locator: Critical minerals: brave capital is needed to unlock supply bottlenecks

insights.claim: Lithium and nickel are harder than copper because China holds dominant positions across processing, refining, battery manufacturing and vehicle production while expanding upstream, and replicating that integrated ecosystem elsewhere will take decades.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: Western lithium/nickel projects face a midstream processing chokepoint they cannot bypass on a decade horizon — mine-only projects without offtake into non-Chinese processing carry hidden risk.
insights.quote: Replicating that ecosystem elsewhere will take decades.
insights.locator: Critical minerals: brave capital is needed to unlock supply bottlenecks

insights.claim: Cobalt and manganese are explicitly not bottleneck risks — incremental cobalt comes as a by-product of DRC copper operations and Indonesian nickel HPAL projects, while the sheer scale of the manganese market absorbs higher demand.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: Screens out cobalt and manganese as EV-scarcity trades; cobalt supply is levered to copper capex, not to its own demand.
insights.locator: Critical minerals: brave capital is needed to unlock supply bottlenecks

insights.claim: Multiple industry interviews for the report produced a consistent message that Western automakers want independent technology and supply chains, yet in the near term the West can only license Chinese technology given Chinese leadership in advanced chemistries.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: Expect a wave of Chinese battery technology licensing deals into Western OEMs — a fee stream for Chinese cell makers and a tell that Western independence is aspirational near term.
insights.quote: Across multiple industry interviews for this edition of Horizons, there was a consistent message: Western automakers desire independent technology and supply chains.
insights.locator: The onus is on the West for technology and supply-chain innovation

insights.claim: Lithium-manganese-rich (LMR) batteries hold the strongest potential for Western-led battery technology through 2040, with advanced LFP and sodium-ion also possible but already targets of aggressive Chinese investment.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: LMR is the named chemistry to track for Western battery differentiation; LFP and sodium-ion bets in the West are racing a better-capitalised Chinese incumbent.
insights.quote: Lithium-manganese-rich (LMR) batteries hold the strongest potential for Western-led battery technology through 2040.
insights.locator: The onus is on the West for technology and supply-chain innovation

insights.claim: The scenario is anchored on Japanese and South Korean battery manufacturers — companies willing to deploy capital into frontier chemistries rather than chase returns on legacy technologies — partnering with Europe and North America, not on Western incumbents innovating alone.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: Japanese and Korean cell makers are the pivotal players in any Western battery independence trade — their capital allocation decisions gate the entire scenario.
insights.quote: Companies from these nations, looking to deploy capital into frontier chemistries rather than chase returns on legacy technologies, anchor our electric shock scenario.
insights.locator: The onus is on the West for technology and supply-chain innovation

insights.claim: Battery supply chain control matters beyond vehicles because the global AI boom is driving a surge in energy storage demand, making battery access a dual-use strategic asset for OECD countries.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: Battery capacity competes between EVs and grid storage for AI data centres — a demand overlay that tightens cell markets beyond auto forecasts.
insights.quote: Battery supply chains could be particularly important in light of the surge in demand for energy storage resulting from the global artificial intelligence (AI) boom.
insights.locator: Staying grounded: how to avoid getting shocked by an EV surge

insights.claim: The positive signposts for EV acceleration are sustained multi-year oil price spikes driven by continued Gulf export disruption, surging Chinese EV exports cutting costs by 2030, and Western policy plus battery advances unleashing domestic manufacturing with smart charging by 2035.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: A dated monitoring checklist — 2030 for Chinese export-driven cost declines, 2035 for Western manufacturing — usable as a scorecard rather than a forecast.
insights.locator: Positive markers for EVs

insights.claim: The single most powerful anti-EV signpost is OPEC deliberately targeting sub-US$60/bbl oil to slow EV sales outside China, explicitly mirroring the strategy that crushed US tight oil production in 2014-16.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: Frames OPEC price policy as an anti-EV weapon with a proven historical precedent — a reason cheap oil could be strategic rather than accidental.
insights.quote: OPEC targets sub-US$60/bbl oil prices, slowing EV sales outside of China, mirroring the strategy that hit US tight oil production in 2014-16.
insights.locator: Negative markers for EVs

insights.claim: Protectionism is modelled as an EV-negative force: local-content mandates and trade tariffs would slow the decline in EV costs through 2035 while leaving battery supply chains dominated by China — protection delays cost parity rather than accelerating domestic capability.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: Tariff escalation is a bearish EV-adoption signal and a bullish gasoline-demand signal — the opposite of how protectionist policy is usually marketed.
insights.locator: Negative markers for EVs

insights.claim: Utility failure to scale managed charging programmes and hold charging costs down through 2040 is listed as a negative marker equal in weight to oil price and tariff risks, making utility execution a first-order determinant of EV adoption.
insights.speaker: David Brown
insights.so_what: Utility software and rate-design execution is an under-priced input to the EV thesis; monitor managed-charging enrolment rates as a leading indicator.
insights.locator: Negative markers for EVs
